issues.legal_issue: A bribery conviction may be based on reliable testimony from a bribe-giver without a fixed requirement of corroboration in material particulars, with the need and extent of corroboration assessed in the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The complainant had to obtain a land title and testified that the senior official demanded a bribe and directed him to hand the money to the assistant.

The complainant approached the vigilance authorities before paying and participated in a trap; the marked money was recovered from the assistant, who admitted receiving it on the senior official’s instructions.

The complainant consistently testified to the demand, had no apparent motive against the senior official, and the surrounding evidence, including testimony from other witnesses, supported the prosecution case.
The assistant claimed he believed the money was repayment of a loan, but the supporting witness established only that a provident-fund loan had been sanctioned.
The trial court and the High Court found both officials guilty, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb those findings.
issues.conclusion: The convictions were upheld. The complainant’s evidence was not subject to an inflexible requirement of corroboration in material particulars, and the recovery and surrounding circumstances supported his account of the demand and payment on the senior official’s instructions.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 133 and 114, Illustration (b), of the Evidence Act permit conviction on an accomplice’s evidence but counsel caution: corroboration is ordinarily sought as a rule of prudence, and whether it is needed depends on the evidence and circumstances. A bribe-giver who is coerced or unwilling and approaches authorities before paying is not automatically to be treated like a willing participant in the crime; the evidence must be carefully assessed, and any corroboration may be circumstantial. The court relied on Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan and King v. Baskerville on accomplice evidence and corroboration; State of Bihar v. Basawan Singh and later decisions including Bhanuprasad Hanprasad Dave, Dalpat Singh, Maha Singh and Hazari Lal on trap witnesses; and distinguished Panalal Damodar Rathi v. State of Maharashtra on its facts.

rule.if: bribery_trap_conviction_appeal and complainant_approached_authorities_before_payment and complainant_testified_to_official_demand and complainant_testimony_was_reliable and money_recovered_from_intermediary and surrounding_evidence_supported_account

predicates.bribery_trap_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction arising from a bribery trap.
predicates.complainant_approached_authorities_befor: The complainant went to the authorities before paying the demanded money.
predicates.complainant_testified_to_official_demand: The complainant testified that an official demanded a bribe.
predicates.complainant_testimony_was_reliable: The court found the complainant’s account sufficiently reliable to act upon.
predicates.money_recovered_from_intermediary: The money paid in the trap was recovered from a person alleged to have received it for an official.
predicates.surrounding_evidence_supported_account: Other evidence or circumstances supported the complainant’s account of the demand or payment.

issues.definition: When a bribery-trap conviction appeal involves a complainant who reported the demand before payment, gives reliable evidence of an official demand, and whose account is supported by recovery and surrounding evidence, the conviction can rest on that testimony and case-specific support.

issues.legal_issue: The custodial sentence for a bribery conviction may be reduced in light of the passage of time, the loss of employment, the hardship of prolonged proceedings, and imprisonment already served.
material_facts: The offences had been committed several years before the appeals were decided.
Both officials had lost their jobs and had endured the criminal proceedings for years.
They had already spent time in jail.
The Supreme Court upheld the convictions and fines but considered it unnecessary to send them back to jail.
issues.conclusion: The imprisonment under each count was reduced to the period already undergone; the fines and default sentences were confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The court exercised its sentencing discretion on the circumstances before it, including the elapsed time, the officials’ loss of employment, the hardship of prolonged proceedings, and the imprisonment already served. It stated no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this modification.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and substantial_time_elapsed_since_offence and accused_lost_employment and accused_endured_prolonged_proceedings and imprisonment_already_served

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction and sentence.
predicates.substantial_time_elapsed_since_offence: A substantial period had passed between the offence and the appellate decision.
predicates.accused_lost_employment: The convicted person had lost their employment.
predicates.accused_endured_prolonged_proceedings: The convicted person had endured lengthy criminal proceedings.
predicates.imprisonment_already_served: The convicted person had already spent time in custody for the offence.

issues.definition: When a conviction appeal involves substantial delay, loss of employment, prolonged proceedings, and imprisonment already served, the custodial sentence may be reduced to the time already served.
